processes.description: A round usually starts when a scheduler, volume analyst or accountant finds gas flowing at a meter or on a pipeline with no valid deal: a ticket expired, ended mid-month or was never created. They email the desk, mostly Daren Farmer, asking for a Sitara deal to be created, extended, zeroed out or corrected. The desk or a logistics coordinator enters or extends the ticket and replies with the deal or track number. The requester then checks that the ticket reflects the flow, so that allocations and the Unify volume drafts can clear.
steps: A scheduler or analyst finds flow at a meter with no deal, an expired ticket or an allocation exception.
They email the desk with the meter, dates, counterparty and any existing deal number.
The desk checks Sitara to see whether the existing deal should be extended or a new one created.
The trader or coordinator creates, extends, zeroes or corrects the ticket in Sitara.
The deal or track number is sent back to the requester.
The requester confirms the ticket is released and flows into Unify so allocations and volume drafts can clear.

stalls.summary: Requesters wait on the desk to enter or release a deal and have to ask again; logistics stays blocked until the trader answers.
Expired or unreleased tickets stop deals from passing into Unify, so volumes cannot be drafted until the ticket is fixed.
Requesters are unsure who can make the change, and requests are passed between people or redirected to another person.
Deal terms are sent with mistakes in the effective date or price and have to be corrected after the first request.

contradictions.summary: Different people are named as the one who puts these deals in: an outside party is told to call Daren Farmer, while another sender says Danny Conner handles it and a third says to talk to Darren.
In the same round, setting up the accounting arrangements is assigned to Volume Management as a group, while Robert E Lloyd splits the months between himself and a colleague.

automation.approach: A daily exception report comparing measured flow and allocation exceptions by meter against active Sitara tickets would flag meters with flow but no deal, and tickets expiring before month end, before anyone has to email. A standard request form would capture meter, dates, counterparty, price and existing deal number, and route to the named owner for that pipeline, with the new deal number returned automatically.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same request missing the same fields (meter, dates, deal number, extend or create), and many stall on who handles it. A structured request form with a routing owner column removes the back-and-forth and the incorrect terms, while the trader still decides whether to extend or create.

work_estimate.rationale: The requester looks up the meter, flow dates and expired ticket; the desk checks Sitara for the existing deal, decides extend or create, enters or corrects the ticket and confirms it reaches Unify. A simple extension takes about 10 minutes; multi-ticket clean-ups and replacement deals take longer, hence the mid of 20. Detection of missing deals and the request fields can be automated; the trading decision and entry review stay manual.

processes.description: Employees submit expense reports in the Concur expense system, which emails the approving manager that a report is ready for approval and later that its approval status has changed. The manager opens the report, reviews it and approves or rejects it. Company announcements push staff to file outstanding expenses through the XMS system and to clear reports waiting in approvers' inboxes.
steps: An employee files an expense report in the expense system.
The system emails the approver that the report is ready for approval.
The approver opens the report and checks the items and receipts.
The approver approves or rejects it, and the system emails the status change.

stalls.summary: An approver away at a class cannot access the system, so reports waiting on that approval stay in the queue.
Reports pile up unprocessed in approvers' inboxes until a company-wide notice asks them to approve or reject them.

automation.approach: The expense system already sends the notifications; an approver checklist and automatic policy checks on receipts, limits and coding would leave the approver reviewing only flagged items, and a delegate approver could cover absences.
automation.rationale: The work is a short review against policy each time; a checklist makes it consistent, and naming a delegate addresses the one stall the mail shows.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round is one report reviewed in the system: open it, check items and receipts against policy, approve or reject. That is a few minutes for a typical report, longer when receipts need questioning. Policy checks could take over part of the review; the decision stays with the approver.

processes.description: Staff or an assistant arrange trips and visits: asking which hotel is nearest the office, booking flights and hotels, and sending the traveller the itinerary or a ticketless airline confirmation. Questions about room details are answered from what the hotel will confirm.
steps: A traveller or visitor asks about travel or hotel options.
Flights and hotel are booked, through the travel agency where used.
The itinerary or ticketless confirmation is sent to the traveller.
Follow-up questions about the booking are answered.

automation.approach: A standard visitor travel note listing nearby hotels, the travel agency contact and booking steps, plus a reusable itinerary message, would cover the repeated questions.
automation.rationale: Rounds are mostly sending the same kinds of information to travellers and visitors, so a reusable message saves the most effort.

work_estimate.rationale: Booking a flight and hotel or looking up hotel options and confirming details takes some minutes per trip; much is handled by the travel agency. A template covers the repeated information, while bookings still need people.
